title: Government technology supplier dependency under scrutiny
headline: Written answers cover government technology supplier dependency, exit planning and open standards, alongside departmental AI model assurance.
summary: Only the Commons sat on Friday 27 November, with private members' bills debated. Written answers describe how departments choose and assure AI models, including Chinese-origin models. Dr Ben Spencer (Conservative) asked about AI governance, while Martin Wrigley (Liberal Democrat), Siân Berry (Green Party) and Clive Lewis (Labour) asked about supplier dependency, exit planning and open standards. Other items cover data-centre energy and regulation, OpenAI's compute and model credits and Anthropic's model credits for the AI Biosecurity Lab, cyber security, digital literacy and committee publications.

very_important.title: Departments outline AI model controls; China assurance questions tabled
very_important.who: Dr Ben Spencer (Conservative, Runnymede and Weybridge), Shadow Minister (Cabinet Office)
very_important.where: Written questions: Department for Education, Ministry of Defence, Treasury, Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, Cabinet Office
very_important.body: Asked whether it uses open-weight AI models published by China-based developers, the Department for Education (Josh MacAlister) said it does not currently do so. It uses AI models made available through approved technology providers and checks every model for data protection, security, cost, availability and capacity before testing or use. The MoD (Luke Pollard) said Chinese-origin models are not permitted for general staff use but that there are 'legitimate Defence use cases', subject to governance, assurance and risk mitigations. Model choice takes account of security and sovereignty requirements. The Treasury said it keeps an internal record of AI models approved for use. On DeepSeek, the Government said it is aware of the US Department of Homeland Security's Exclusion and Removal Order #2026-01 and regularly engages industry about international regulatory developments. On 27 November Dr Spencer tabled three new questions asking when China-model security-assurance results will be shared with businesses, which body is doing the work and whether DeepSeek is covered. His questions refer to security-assurance work on AI models from China mentioned by the Minister for Artificial Intelligence in the House on 26 November.
very_important.why: The answers describe departmental AI checks and the MoD's security and sovereignty considerations. The newly tabled questions seek details of China-model assurance work; no answers are supplied.

very_important.title: HMRC and Post Office asked about dependency on Accenture, Capgemini, CGI and Fujitsu
very_important.who: Siân Berry (Green Party, Brighton Pavilion), Green Party Chief Whip
very_important.where: Written questions: Treasury; Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
very_important.body: Ms Berry asked, supplier by supplier, about HMRC's assessment of technical, commercial and operational dependency risks involving Accenture, Capgemini, CGI and Fujitsu, and about exit planning and assessment of insourcing. The Treasury (James Murray) gave the same answer each time. HMRC manages these risks through contract, supplier and technology governance, resilience arrangements, knowledge retention and transfer, and transition and exit planning. Technology modernisation offers opportunities to reduce reliance on ageing systems and concentrated expertise. Detailed contract exit and contingency arrangements are commercially sensitive and are not disclosed. On the Post Office, the Government (Kate Dearden) said it is providing up to £483 million over 2026-27 and 2027-28 for transformation, including the transition away from Fujitsu and replacement of Horizon. The answer says Post Office recently announced a short, final Fujitsu contract extension to maintain continuity while Accenture takes over Horizon support.
very_important.why: The answers describe supplier-risk management and the Post Office's transition arrangements. HMRC does not disclose detailed contract exit and contingency arrangements.

very_important.title: GDS role in reducing supplier lock-in; National Cloud Infrastructure Programme cited
very_important.where: Written questions: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
very_important.body: Mr Lewis asked about the Government Digital Service's (GDS) role in managing risks from long-term dependence on a limited number of technology suppliers. The Government (Stephanie Peacock) said GDS works across government on supplier-dependency risks, 'including lock-in, resilience, portability and interoperability'. It works with the Government Commercial Function and Government Commercial Agency because these risks require commercial as well as technical action. The Digital Commercial Centre of Excellence brings this expertise together, including through the National Cloud Infrastructure Programme, which aims to strengthen competition, resilience and choice. A second answer said the Government is committed to giving open-source software equal consideration alongside proprietary options. It states: 'Code built with public money should be open and reusable by default.' Departments must demonstrate that they have considered open-source software; compliance is monitored through service assessments and spend controls.
very_important.why: The answer identifies supplier dependency, portability and interoperability as risks managed jointly through technical and commercial work. It cites the National Cloud Infrastructure Programme's aims of competition, resilience and choice.

very_important.title: FCDO lists African supply-chain contact routes
very_important.where: Written question: Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office
very_important.body: In reply to a question on connecting UK businesses with African manufacturers and suppliers, the FCDO (Kirsty McNeill) listed the Manufacturing Africa and Growth Gateway programmes and provided contact routes for programme delivery partners.
very_important.why: The answer identifies programmes supporting business connections and routes for exploring participation.

debates.title: SLAPP (No. 2) Bill second reading: legal threats over social media posts
debates.who: Sir John Whittingdale (Conservative, Maldon); Alicia Kearns (Conservative); Alex Sobel (Labour/Co-op); Graeme Downie (Labour); Sarah Sackman for the Government
debates.body: Sir John moved the second reading of his bill to protect defendants against strategic lawsuits against public participation (SLAPPs). Members described people threatened with legal action over Facebook and Instagram posts. Sarah Sackman supported the bill and said it creates an early dismissal mechanism: a court could strike out a claim meeting the SLAPP test where the claimant cannot show it is more likely than not to succeed and the public interest favours dismissal. She said she had worked with Sir John on the bill. Members also discussed hybrid threats, including cyber attacks.
debates.why: The debate connects protection against abusive litigation with speech on social media. Members from different parties expressed support for the bill.

questions.title: AI governance: OpenAI and Anthropic credits, AI Taskforce and supplier choice
questions.who: Dr Ben Spencer (Conservative, Runnymede and Weybridge)
questions.body: Kanishka Narayan said OpenAI has committed £100 million in compute and model credits and Anthropic up to £100 million in model credits for the AI Biosecurity Lab, up to £200 million collectively. Asked about the Prime Minister's AI Taskforce's role in supplier choice, he said individual contracting authorities are responsible for their procurement decisions within procurement legislation. The Taskforce does not intend to publish regular milestones; progress and key milestones will be communicated when appropriate. The answer on a possible new AI strategy did not confirm whether one is planned. New questions tabled on 27 November ask whether the Minister for Artificial Intelligence has approved a work programme for the GovAI Unit and when the transfer of staff from the former Department for Science, Innovation and Technology to the Cabinet Office will be complete.
questions.why: The answers describe credits for the AI Biosecurity Lab and contracting authorities' procurement responsibilities. They do not rule out a wider role for the AI Taskforce.

questions.title: Compute Roadmap modelling and AI Growth Zones investment
questions.who: Dr Ben Spencer (Conservative, Runnymede and Weybridge)
questions.where: Written questions: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
questions.body: The Government said the Compute Roadmap, published in July 2025, forecasts a need for at least 6GW of AI-capable data-centre capacity by 2030. The scenario-based modelling behind that forecast was published in the Roadmap's Compute Evidence Annex. More than £28 billion of private investment has been committed to AI Growth Zones, a figure supplied by the companies themselves. The answer does not give a total spent to date and says the Government does not publish commercially sensitive details of how individual companies structure their investments over time.
questions.why: The answers distinguish forecast compute demand and committed investment from expenditure already incurred. No spending total is supplied.

questions.title: Data Centre Covenant: public-service compute and proposed NIS regulation
questions.where: Written question: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
questions.body: Asked about securing public-service compute under point 5 of the Treasury's Data Centre Covenant, which the question dates to 28 October 2026, the Government (Kanishka Narayan) said the Covenant sets five tests that all data centres are encouraged to meet. These include security and resilience expectations for compute relied on by critical services. The Government is discussing implementation with industry and national technical authorities. Hosts in the AI Research Resource must meet strict cyber-security, service-continuity and recovery requirements. The Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill would bring relevant data centres into the NIS regime as essential services, regulated by Ofcom.
questions.why: The Covenant encourages data centres to meet its tests. The bill would introduce Ofcom-regulated security and resilience requirements for relevant data centres.

questions.title: Data Centre Commitment Fee and trade unions in frontier AI and Big Tech
questions.who: Dame Chi Onwurah (Labour, Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West), Science and Technology Committee member
questions.where: Written questions: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero; Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
questions.body: Dame Chi asked about the potential impact of viable data-centre projects being paused or withdrawn from the connection queue because of the proposed level of the Data Centre Commitment Fee. Michael Shanks said speculative data-centre applications are delaying strategically important demand projects and that the Government supports measures to ensure scarce capacity is held by credible, deliverable projects. Ofgem's proposed fee would be a refundable deposit; its design is for Ofgem, and a decision will be published in due course. Asked separately about the merits of trade union membership in frontier AI and Big Tech companies, the Government (Kate Dearden) said it has made no sector-specific assessment but that unions play an 'essential role'.
questions.why: The fee remains an Ofgem proposal awaiting a decision. Dame Chi's separate question seeks the Government's assessment of trade union membership in frontier AI and Big Tech companies.

questions.title: How many Labour MPs have raised concerns about data centres and energy infrastructure
questions.who: John Lamont (Conservative, Berwickshire, Roxburgh and Selkirk), Shadow Deputy Leader of the House of Commons
questions.where: Written question (tabled, not yet answered): Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
questions.body: Mr Lamont asked how many Labour MPs have raised concerns with the department about solar farms, wind farms, battery storage, data centres and other electricity infrastructure in their constituencies.
questions.why: The question seeks a count of Labour MPs who have raised constituency infrastructure concerns. No answer is supplied.

questions.title: Cost of significant cyber attacks to business put at £14.7 billion; £150 million for cyber defence
questions.who: James MacCleary (Liberal Democrat, Lewes), Liberal Democrat defence spokesperson
questions.where: Written question: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
questions.body: Chris McDonald said government-commissioned research puts the cost of significant cyber attacks to UK businesses at about £14.7 billion in 2024, around 0.5% of UK GDP. This is an indicative estimate based predominantly on US attack-cost data combined with UK data on businesses estimated to experience such attacks. He pointed to the £150 million for cyber defence announced at the Budget, covering a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability Centre, expanded public-sector AI cyber defence and a national Cyber Shield.
questions.why: The answer records an indicative cyber-cost estimate and the Budget's cyber-defence funding priorities. It supplies no procurement details.

questions.title: AI security priorities for the UK's 2027 G20 Presidency
questions.who: Victoria Collins (Liberal Democrat, Harpenden and Berkhamsted), Liberal Democrat science, innovation and technology spokesperson
questions.where: Written question: Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office
questions.body: Ms Collins asked whether the UK's 2027 G20 Presidency will prioritise the cyber security of AI systems, AI-enabled cyber attacks and the resilience of critical national infrastructure. Chris Elmore said AI will be 'at the heart' of the Presidency, covering opportunities and risks. Full policy priorities will be shared after the Miami Summit.
questions.why: The answer commits to placing AI at the heart of the UK Presidency but does not confirm the three specific security priorities asked about.

questions.title: AI and the tech workforce; schools' MIS procurement framework
questions.where: Written questions: Cabinet Office; Department for Education
questions.body: Kanishka Narayan said there is currently 'no clear evidence' of widespread job displacement attributable to AI across the UK labour market, but this could change as capabilities advance. The AI Economics Institute will continue assessing employment and wage implications. Separately, DfE said its management information system (MIS) procurement framework is expected to be available from September 2027. Schools will then be able to award contracts with start dates suited to their needs. Existing contracts may continue to expiry, with available extensions used where necessary to bridge the period before the framework is available. Schools are expected to award their next MIS contract through the framework when existing contracts expire.
questions.why: The answers describe continued assessment of AI's labour-market effects and an expected timetable and procurement route for school MIS contracts.

questions.title: Workplace surveillance technology and platform-economy working conditions
questions.who: Chris Bloore (Labour, Redditch), Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee member
questions.where: Written questions: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
questions.body: The Government (Kate Dearden) said its consultation on workplace monitoring technologies recognised 'legitimate concerns' about surveillance; a response will follow in due course. A consultation on employment status and protections for the self-employed, relevant to platform workers, closes on 8 January 2027. Related questions from Rachel Gilmour (Liberal Democrat) and Neil Duncan-Jordan (Labour) on Royal Mail's monitoring technology and Postal Digital Assistants received similar responses on workplace surveillance.
questions.why: The answers describe consultations on workplace monitoring and employment status. The latter closes on 8 January 2027; no final outcomes of those consultations are supplied.

questions.title: Digital media literacy in schools and harmful algorithms
questions.where: Written questions: Department for Education; Department of Health and Social Care (tabled)
questions.body: DfE said schools have been required to follow the revised relationships, sex and health education statutory guidance since September. It says secondary pupils should learn to assess online information critically and recognise misinformation and disinformation, and it covers AI and identifying deepfakes and their harms. The National Centre for Computing Education offers free professional development on digital literacy and AI. Media and digital literacy will be included in consultation on the new curriculum. A newly tabled question asks about assessment of harmful online content and social media algorithms' impact on the mental health of boys and young men.
questions.why: Existing statutory guidance covers AI and deepfakes; wider digital and media literacy reforms are to be included in curriculum consultation.

questions.title: Cross-government data sharing and the National Data Library
questions.where: Written question: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
questions.body: The Government (Stephanie Peacock) pointed to Digital Economy Act gateways, new public-service delivery objectives, common standards and shared infrastructure, including common reference data and the API Mandate. It said the National Data Library is being developed to make public-sector data easier to find and use.
questions.why: The answer describes common standards and infrastructure intended to improve public-sector data discovery and reuse. It gives no procurement details.

questions.title: £750 million national supercomputer in Edinburgh
questions.where: Written question: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
questions.body: Asked about UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) budgeting for new research infrastructure, the Government (Chris McDonald) repeated the Spending Review 2025 commitment of £750 million for a new national supercomputer in Edinburgh, alongside upkeep of existing facilities.
questions.why: The answer records a national research-computing funding commitment alongside maintenance of existing research facilities.

questions.title: Home Office AI facial age estimation: testing and data source
questions.where: Written questions (tabled, not yet answered): Home Office
questions.body: Ms Begum asked what testing expectations must be met before AI facial age estimation is operationalised to support initial age decisions. Separately, citing an earlier answer, she asked about the source and lawful processing basis of 2.5 million operational images used to test industry algorithms.
questions.why: The questions seek testing and data-processing details. No answers are supplied.

questions.title: Enforcing platform-to-business rules for small firms
questions.where: Written question (tabled, not yet answered): Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
questions.body: Mr Morris asked about the effectiveness of the Online Intermediation Services for Business Users (Enforcement) Regulations 2020 in enabling small businesses to enforce rights under the Platform-to-Business Regulation. He also asked whether the Government has considered establishing an independent regulator or ombudsman to investigate complaints and enforce compliance without court action.
questions.why: The question seeks an assessment of enforcement and consideration of an independent complaints body. No answer is supplied.

questions.title: AI firms' borrowing costs and safety by design in wearable tech
questions.where: Lords written questions: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade; Home Office
questions.body: Baroness Lloyd of Effra said the Bank of England has statutory responsibility for monetary policy and financial stability and operational independence. The Government aims to maintain economic stability so domestic AI firms can attract investment and scale up. On discreet wearable filming devices, Lord Hanson of Flint said technology companies are expected to build in privacy and safety 'from the outset'. He said the Government will consider whether existing safeguards are adequate and that 'All options remain on the table'.
questions.why: The wearable-technology answer describes safety and privacy expectations and consideration of existing safeguards. It does not announce new duties.

questions.title: Misleading online advertising and consumer law
questions.who: Chris Coghlan (Liberal Democrat, Dorking and Horley)
questions.where: Written question: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
questions.body: On misleading online adverts for accident management services, the Government said the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 prohibits unfair commercial practices, including misleading actions and omissions likely to affect the average consumer's transactional decision. It said the Advertising Standards Authority independently regulates advertising.
questions.why: The answer identifies existing consumer law and independent advertising regulation.

committees.who: Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, to the committee Chair
committees.where: Committee correspondence (Afghan Data Breach and Resettlement Schemes inquiry)
committees.body: A letter dated 18 November about the Government's response to the Afghan data breach and resettlement schemes report was published. Separately, the Treasury (Lord Pitt-Watson) told Lord Kempsell (Conservative) that guidance to accounting officers on sharing information covered by injunctions was published in full on 28 July 2026.
committees.why: The correspondence and written answer concern the Government's response to the breach report and guidance on sharing information covered by injunctions.

other.title: Grid demand, energy security and the UK Cooling Outlook
other.who: Lee Anderson (Reform UK, Ashfield); Paul Holmes (Conservative, Hamble Valley)
other.where: Written questions (tabled, not yet answered): Department for Energy Security and Net Zero; Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs
other.body: Mr Anderson asked about assessment of increased demand's impact on the ageing grid and energy security. Mr Holmes asked when the UK Cooling Outlook strategy will be published. Neither question mentions data centres.
other.why: These are energy-system and cooling-policy questions, not explicit questions about data centres.

other.title: Next-generation AR/VR helmet for the Global Combat Air Programme
other.who: Ben Obese-Jecty (Conservative, Huntingdon), Shadow Parliamentary Under Secretary (Defence)
other.where: Written question (tabled, not yet answered): Ministry of Defence
other.body: Mr Obese-Jecty asked about progress on the next-generation augmented and virtual reality helmet for GCAP. In a separate question, he asked which required operational effects need a crewed platform. No supplier is named in either question.
other.why: The questions concern helmet development and operational requirements for crewed platforms.

other.title: Capita pension contract; hostile state activity including cyber
other.who: Mike Wood (Conservative, Kingswinford and South Staffordshire); Stuart Anderson (Conservative, South Shropshire)
other.where: Written questions: Cabinet Office (tabled); Ministry of Defence
other.body: Mr Wood asked for the full Capita contract for administering the Civil Service Pension Scheme to be placed in the Library, including the schedule of financial corrections against Capita. In an answer to Mr Anderson, the MoD cited MI5's Director General as saying that the Security Service's work on state threats has quadrupled over the past decade. The answer says such activity includes cyber activity, often conducted below the threshold of armed conflict.
other.why: The items concern disclosure of an outsourced public-service contract and the Government's account of hostile-state cyber activity.

coverage: Period: from an unspecified start date to Friday 27 November 2026.
Friday 27 November: only the Commons sat. Supplied Hansard covers the private members' SLAPP (No. 2) Bill and Ceramics (Country of Origin Marking) Bill debates; the Lords did not sit.

Screened 705 written questions and answers and 3 written statements. One statement is supplied, on water customer support. The evidence also includes Commons Hansard for 27 November and 14 committee publications.
No parliamentary business was listed for Saturday 28 November, so there is no Today section.
No data warnings or source gaps were reported.
